passage: In the nursery-school garden, four children were building a mud house. Nandini ran over with a stick for the roof. Vaibhav stood in front of it. "You can't play with us." The others nodded. Nandini felt a stone drop into her tummy. Her eyes filled. She walked slowly to Mrs Kurian by the gate. "They said I can't play." Mrs Kurian held her hand. "That hurt. It's not because of anything wrong with you." She walked Nandini back. "Builders, you need someone to make windows. Nandini has a stick. Where shall she start?" Vaibhav pointed at the wall.

qa.q: What did Nandini bring for the mud house?
qa.a: She brought a stick for the roof.

qa.q: How did Nandini feel when Vaibhav said she couldn't play?
qa.a: She felt hurt and rejected, like a stone dropped into her tummy, and tears came.

qa.q: How did Mrs Kurian make a place for Nandini?
qa.a: She comforted her, said it wasn't her fault, and gave her a useful job making windows so the group had a reason to include her.

qa.q: How might Vaibhav see Nandini when she comes back with a job?
qa.a: He may start to see her as a helper for the house rather than an outsider, so pointing to a wall feels easy.

grounding: A young girl is told she can't play, feels hurt, tells a teacher, and the teacher helps make a place for her.

passage:
Monday: "You can't play with us," Rafiq said at the swings. Ishita's tummy felt like it had a stone in it. She sat on the step and cried.
Tuesday: Ishita saw the swings were full of the same group. She took a breath and went to the sandpit instead. Two younger children were digging. She helped them make a well.
Thursday: She told Miss Joshi about Monday. Miss Joshi started a parachute game for everyone. "Ishita, hold this side. Rafiq, that side." Ishita laughed when the parachute puffed up.

qa.q: What did Ishita help make in the sandpit?
qa.a: She helped two younger children make a well.

qa.q: How did Ishita feel on Monday?
qa.a: She felt hurt and sad, with a stone in her tummy, so she sat on the step and cried.

qa.q: What two wise steps did Ishita take after being left out?
qa.a: She found another game in the sandpit, and she told Miss Joshi, who made a place for her in a game everyone could join.

qa.q: What is it like for Rafiq to hold the parachute with Ishita?
qa.a: He finds himself playing alongside her in a fun game, which may soften his idea that she can't join. 🙂

grounding: Over a few days, a girl told she can't play feels hurt, finds another game, tells a teacher, and the teacher makes a place for her.

passage:
Note from the Sunflower class teacher, for Aparna's parents.
At break Aparna told Seema, "No you. You can't come in our house." Then she told the other girls, "Nobody plays with Seema, that's the rule." She looked very pleased with herself. Seema sat on the bench and cried. I took Aparna aside. I asked, "How would you feel if your friends made a rule against you?" She went quiet and looked at Seema. After a minute she walked over and said, "Come and play." I told the group we don't make rules to leave people out.

qa.q: What rule did Aparna try to make?
qa.a: She told the other girls, "Nobody plays with Seema, that's the rule."

qa.q: Why did Aparna look pleased with herself?
qa.a: Leaving Seema out made her feel powerful in her group; she had not yet understood how much it hurt.

qa.q: How did the teacher help Aparna change?
qa.a: The teacher asked her to imagine how she would feel, which helped her see Seema's side and invite her, and then told the group no leaving-out rules.

qa.q: How might Seema feel when Aparna says "Come and play"?
qa.a: Seema may feel relieved but still a bit wary, since Aparna was the one who left her out.

grounding: A young girl excludes a classmate to feel powerful and tries to make it a group rule, and a teacher helps her imagine the hurt and invite her in.

passage: By the village pond, the girls were playing hopscotch with a flat stone. Mehak came running. Devika spread her arms. "No you! Only us." Mehak's face fell and she turned away. Devika giggled with the others. Their teacher, Madhuri Ma'am, was walking back from the school. She knelt by Devika. "Look at Mehak's face. What do you think she feels?" Devika looked. Mehak was rubbing her eyes by the tree. "Sad," Devika said slowly. "What could make her feel better?" Devika picked up the flat stone and ran to the tree. "Mehak, come and play. You can throw first."

qa.q: What were the girls using for hopscotch?
qa.a: They were using a flat stone.

qa.q: How did Devika feel when she spread her arms and said "No you"?
qa.a: She felt powerful and giggly with her group, and did not yet understand how it hurt Mehak.

qa.q: Which question from Madhuri Ma'am helped Devika most?
qa.a: Asking "What do you think she feels?" made Devika look at Mehak's sad face and imagine her hurt, which led her to invite Mehak.

qa.q: How might Mehak see Devika's invitation to throw first?
qa.a: She may feel surprised and happy to be welcomed after being turned away. 😊

grounding: A young girl leaves another child out to feel powerful, and a teacher helps her imagine the hurt and invite her in.

passage: In the school yard in Porto, the children ran in twos and threes. Priscila stood by the fence, holding her lunchbox. Nobody called her name. Nobody bumped into her. It was like she wasn't there. At pick-up, her mother, Rosa, saw her eyes. "Who did you play with?" Priscila shrugged. "Nobody sees me." Rosa hugged her. "That sounds lonely. It's not your fault. Let's practise something. You say, 'Hi, can I see?' to someone building." Priscila tried it in the car. "And Saturday, shall we invite Inês from your class to the park?" Priscila nodded.

qa.q: What was Priscila holding by the fence?
qa.a: Priscila was holding her lunchbox.

qa.q: What was Priscila feeling when she said "Nobody sees me"?
qa.a: She felt lonely and invisible, as if she wasn't there at all.

qa.q: What two ways did Rosa help without shaming her?
qa.a: She practised a friendly line with Priscila and planned a small play date at the park with a classmate.

qa.q: How might Rosa feel when she sees Priscila's eyes at pick-up?
qa.a: She may feel a pang of sadness for her daughter and a wish to help gently.

grounding: A young girl feels invisible on the playground, and her mother helps her practise a friendly line and plans a play date.

passage: During outdoor time at the kindergarten, Gopika leaned against the drinking-water tank. The others raced past chasing a ball. Nobody looked at her. She scratched a pattern in the dust with her shoe. Her teacher, Chandrika Miss, came and stood beside her. "Busy playground today. Shall we practise a friendly line? 'Can I be on your team?'" Gopika whispered it. "Once more, with a smile." Gopika tried again. "Now let's find a small group." They walked to two girls sorting leaves. "Can I be on your team?" Gopika asked. One of them handed her a yellow leaf.

qa.q: What were the two girls sorting?
qa.a: The two girls were sorting leaves.

qa.q: How can you tell Gopika felt invisible?
qa.a: Nobody looked at her, and she stood alone scratching the dust with her shoe while others raced past.

qa.q: Why did Chandrika Miss choose a small group rather than the ball game?
qa.a: A small, calm group was a safer first try for a shy child than a noisy crowd racing past.

qa.q: How might the girl who handed Gopika a leaf see her?
qa.a: She may see a friendly new teammate and feel pleased to share. 🙂

grounding: A young girl stands unnoticed on the playground, and a teacher helps her practise a friendly line and join a small group.

passage:
"Charu! Come, you can be the goalkeeper!" Sharmila shouted across the park.
Charu stopped. "Me?"
"Yes, you! Quick, before they score!"
Charu ran and stood between the two slippers that made the goal. The ball rolled towards her and she fell on it. "Saved it!" everyone yelled.
On the way home Charu told Mumma, "Sharmila picked me. My tummy went all warm."
"How nice. Who else was watching?"
"A little boy by the bench." Charu thought. "Tomorrow I'll ask him to be the other goalkeeper."

qa.q: What did the children use to make the goal?
qa.a: They used two slippers to make the goal.

qa.q: How did Charu feel when Sharmila picked her?
qa.a: She felt warm relief and happiness, as if she belonged in the game.

qa.q: What does Charu plan to do tomorrow, and why is it wise?
qa.a: She plans to invite the little boy by the bench, passing on the welcome she received.

qa.q: How might Sharmila see Charu's save?
qa.a: Sharmila probably feels glad and proud she picked Charu.

grounding: A young girl is welcomed into a game as goalkeeper, feels warm relief, and decides to invite another child next time.

passage:
From the class teacher's note to Damini's parents.
Damini has been standing near the football group for three days, not asking. Today Divyansh saw her and called, "Come, you can be the goalkeeper!" She ran so fast her ponytail flew. She stopped two balls and the whole team cheered. At lunch she said, "Divyansh asked me. I felt like I was in the team." Then something lovely happened: a new boy sat alone, and Damini went and asked him to play. You might like to ask her about it tonight. 🙂

qa.q: How many balls did Damini stop?
qa.a: She stopped two balls.

qa.q: What does Damini's comment "I felt like I was in the team" suggest?
qa.a: She felt relieved and warm, as if she finally belonged after days of standing near the group.

qa.q: How could Damini's parents encourage what she did next?
qa.a: They could ask her about inviting the new boy and tell her that passing on a welcome is kind and brave.

qa.q: How might Divyansh feel when Damini stops the balls?
qa.a: He may feel pleased and proud that his invitation worked out so well.

grounding: A young girl who stood on the edge is welcomed as goalkeeper, feels she belongs, and then welcomes a new child herself.

passage:
Monday: At break, Simran sat alone on the steps, picking at her shoelace. The teacher, Mrs Nair, sat down beside her and said nothing for a bit. Then she asked, "Want to help me count the ducks on the pond?"
Tuesday: Mrs Nair and Simran were counting again when Imran came over. "What are you counting?" "Ducks. Want to help?" Mrs Nair asked. Imran squatted beside Simran. "I see seven!"
Friday: Simran and Imran counted ducks by themselves. Mrs Nair waved from the gate and did not come over.

qa.q: How many ducks did Imran count?
qa.a: Imran said, "I see seven!"

qa.q: What was Simran feeling when she sat on the steps?
qa.a: She felt lonely and alone, picking at her shoelace while others played.

qa.q: How did Mrs Nair help without embarrassing Simran?
qa.a: She sat beside her quietly, offered a simple job and let another child join naturally, without forcing anyone to be friends.

qa.q: Why might Mrs Nair stay back at the gate on Friday?
qa.a: She can see Simran is less lonely now, so she steps back and lets the friendship grow on its own.

grounding: Over a week, a teacher sits beside a lonely child and gently lets others join, without embarrassing her or forcing friendship.

passage: It was raining, so thirty children were crammed into the hall for break. Lalremsiami sat under the stage stairs, knees up, alone. Miss Thanga had a pile of spilled crayons to sort and a crying child to comfort. Still she came over and sat on the floor beside Lalremsiami. "It's loud today. Want to be my crayon helper?" Lalremsiami nodded. They sorted blues and reds. Divyansh wandered over. "Can I sort green?" Miss Thanga smiled. "Ask Lalremsiami, she's the boss." Lalremsiami held out the green pile.

qa.q: What was Miss Thanga sorting?
qa.a: She had a pile of spilled crayons to sort.

qa.q: How did Lalremsiami feel under the stairs?
qa.a: She felt lonely and alone in the loud, crowded hall.

qa.q: What did Miss Thanga do that was wise, even though she was busy?
qa.a: She sat beside her without drawing attention, gave her a helper job, and let Divyansh join by asking Lalremsiami instead of ordering anyone.

qa.q: How might Divyansh see Lalremsiami after being told she's the boss?
qa.a: Divyansh may see her as someone with something fun to share, not as the child alone under the stairs.

grounding: On a crowded rainy day, a busy teacher sits beside a lonely child and gently helps another child join, without embarrassing her.

passage:
Monday: A bigger boy, Lalit, pushed Sabina against the wall and took her biscuit packet. "Don't tell," he said. Sabina's legs shook.
Tuesday: Lalit took her pencil box. "Don't tell, or else." Sabina did not eat her lunch.
That evening she cried into Ammi's lap. "He said don't tell." Ammi held her close. "You were right to tell me. It's not your fault. Telling is safe." Ammi phoned the class teacher right then and explained.
Wednesday: The teacher kept Lalit near her at break. Sabina's pencil box came back.

qa.q: What did Lalit take on Tuesday?
qa.a: Lalit took Sabina's pencil box.

qa.q: Why did Sabina not eat her lunch on Tuesday?
qa.a: She was scared of Lalit and worried about what would happen if she told.

qa.q: What did Ammi do that same evening?
qa.a: She comforted Sabina, told her it wasn't her fault and that telling is safe, and phoned the class teacher right then.

qa.q: How might the class teacher see Ammi's phone call?
qa.a: The teacher likely feels grateful to know and responsible to act, which is why Lalit was kept close the next day.

grounding: A young girl is pushed and robbed by a bigger child who says don't tell, tells her mother, and the adults act the same day.

passage: The school van was packed and the driver was busy with the traffic. A big boy at the back grabbed Yash's crayon box and shoved him into the window. "Don't tell anyone, baby." Yash held his arm and stared out, scared. When the van reached school, Sabina Ma'am was at the gate. Yash's lip wobbled. "He took my crayons. He pushed me. He said don't tell." Sabina Ma'am knelt. "Thank you for telling me. You did nothing wrong." She went straight to the van, got the crayons back, and took the big boy to the office. She sent a note home to Yash's parents that afternoon.

qa.q: Where was Sabina Ma'am when the van reached school?
qa.a: Sabina Ma'am was at the gate.

qa.q: How was Yash feeling as he stared out of the window?
qa.a: He felt scared and hurt, and unsure whether he was allowed to tell.

qa.q: What did Sabina Ma'am do that made telling safe?
qa.a: She thanked Yash, said he did nothing wrong, acted at once to get the crayons back, took the boy to the office and told his parents that afternoon.

qa.q: What would change if Yash had kept quiet?
qa.a: The big boy might keep pushing him and taking his things, and Yash would stay frightened on every van ride.

grounding: A small boy is pushed by a bigger child who says don't tell, tells a teacher anyway, and she believes him and acts.

passage: At the community centre's painting club, Sahil said, "My thun is yellow." A boy at the next table copied him loudly: "Thun! Thun!" The others laughed. Sahil's ears went hot and his eyes stung. He put down his brush and walked away to the window. Then he went to Hafsa, the club helper. "They're laughing at how I talk." Hafsa knelt. "That's not okay, and it's not about you. Thank you for telling me." She went to the table. "In this club, nobody makes fun of anyone." She stayed near Sahil the rest of the session and told his father at pick-up.

qa.q: What did Sahil say about his sun?
qa.a: He said, "My thun is yellow."

qa.q: How was Sahil feeling when his ears went hot?
qa.a: He felt small, hurt and embarrassed as the others laughed at how he talks.

qa.q: Which two wise choices did Sahil make?
qa.a: He walked away from the mocking and told Hafsa, a trusted adult, instead of staying silent.

qa.q: How might the laughing children see Hafsa's rule?
qa.a: They may feel a bit ashamed and realise that copying Sahil hurt him, not just made a joke.

grounding: A young boy is mocked for how he talks, walks away and tells a trusted adult, who acts the same day.

passage:
Monday: A girl in class called Abhinav "four-eyes" because of his new glasses. Others giggled. Abhinav said nothing. He took his glasses off and squinted all day.
Tuesday: "Four-eyes!" again. Abhinav's eyes went hot. He sat in the toilet at break so nobody would see.
Wednesday: When it started, he walked away and went to Gopika Ma'am. "They call me four-eyes." Gopika Ma'am said, "I believe you. That's about them, not you." She spoke to the class that morning and phoned his mother after school.
Friday: Abhinav wore his glasses all day.

qa.q: What did the girl call Abhinav?
qa.a: She called him "four-eyes" because of his new glasses.

qa.q: Why did Abhinav hide in the toilet at break on Tuesday?
qa.a: He felt hurt and ashamed, hot-eyed, and did not want anyone to see him upset.

qa.q: What went wrong on Monday and Tuesday, and what changed?
qa.a: Staying silent let the hurt grow; on Wednesday he walked away and told Gopika Ma'am, who believed him and acted that day.

qa.q: How might Abhinav's mother feel after Gopika Ma'am's phone call?
qa.a: She may feel sad he was hurt, but relieved the teacher believed him and acted quickly.

grounding: Over a week, a young boy mocked for his glasses stops staying silent, walks away and tells a trusted teacher who acts.

passage: Near the village well, Pappu kept pulling Mehak's plait and singing "Mehak smells like goats!" The other children laughed. Mehak said nothing. Her chest felt tight and helpless. Then she hit Pappu hard on the arm. He yelled. Nazia Ma'am from the school came running. "Mehak, no hitting." Mehak stood with her fists shaking. Nazia Ma'am knelt down. "Now tell me, what made you so upset?" Mehak told her about the song. Nazia Ma'am nodded. "That was unkind of Pappu. Next time, shout 'Stop!' and come to me. I'll help."

qa.q: What did Pappu sing about Mehak?
qa.a: He sang "Mehak smells like goats!"

qa.q: How was Mehak feeling before she hit Pappu?
qa.a: She felt helpless and hurt, her chest tight, as the teasing and laughter went on.

qa.q: What could Mehak do next time instead of hitting?
qa.a: She could shout "Stop!" loudly and go to Nazia Ma'am for help.

qa.q: How might Nazia Ma'am see the hit once Mehak explains?
qa.a: She still says hitting is wrong, but she understands Mehak was pushed too far and sees Pappu's teasing needs dealing with too.

grounding: A young girl hits a boy who teased her, gets into trouble, and the teacher both sets the rule and asks what upset her.

passage: In the kindergarten in Hamburg, Hiroshi kept knocking down Kwame's towers and saying, "Baby blocks!" Kwame told him to stop once, very quietly. Hiroshi laughed and did it again. Kwame felt small and trapped. He shoved Hiroshi so hard he fell over. Frau Weber came and took Kwame to the thinking chair. Kwame cried. After a while she sat beside him. "Pushing hurt Hiroshi. What happened before?" Kwame told her about the towers. "That wasn't fair. Next time say 'STOP!' in a big voice and come to me straight away."

qa.q: What did Hiroshi say when he knocked down the towers?
qa.a: He said, "Baby blocks!"

qa.q: Why did Kwame shove Hiroshi?
qa.a: He felt small, trapped and helpless after his quiet stop did not work, and pushing seemed the only answer.

qa.q: What did Frau Weber do that was wise after the push?
qa.a: She gave a consequence, then sat with Kwame and asked what happened before, and taught him to say STOP loudly and fetch her.

qa.q: What is it like for Hiroshi when he falls over?
qa.a: He is hurt and probably shocked, and he may not have realised how much his teasing upset Kwame.

grounding: A young boy pushes a child who kept teasing him, gets in trouble, and the teacher also asks what made him so upset.

passage: In the colony school's corridor, Ishita tugged her teacher's sari. "Lakshmi Miss, a big girl in the lift keeps pinching me and taking my hair clips." Lakshmi Miss put down her books and crouched. "Show me where." Ishita showed the red marks on her arm. "Thank you for telling me. I believe you." That same day, Lakshmi Miss spoke to the big girl and her class teacher, and told Ishita's mother at pick-up. Next morning, a teacher rode in the lift. Ishita breathed out. Her shoulders came down. "Telling worked," she told her friend.

qa.q: What was the big girl taking from Ishita?
qa.a: She was taking Ishita's hair clips.

qa.q: How did Ishita feel the next morning in the lift?
qa.a: She felt relieved and safe; her shoulders came down and she breathed out.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi Miss do that made Ishita feel safe to speak up?
qa.a: She stopped, looked at the marks, said "I believe you," and acted the same day with the other teacher and Ishita's mother.

qa.q: How might Ishita's mother feel when told at pick-up?
qa.a: She may feel upset about the pinching but grateful the teacher believed Ishita and acted fast. 🙏

grounding: A young girl tells her teacher about being hurt by a bigger girl, is believed, and feels relief when the teacher acts.

passage:
"Bhavna Ma'am, can I tell you something?"
"Of course, Ganga. Sit here."
"Rohit says my tiffin smells bad. Every day. He throws it on the floor."
"Every day? That must feel awful."
"You believe me?"
"I believe you. Thank you for telling me. It isn't your fault."
"Will he be angry?"
"I'll make sure you're safe. I'll talk to him and his parents today, and I'll sit near you at lunch."
At lunch, Bhavna Ma'am pulled up a chair next to Ganga. Rohit ate quietly. Ganga opened her tiffin and smiled.

qa.q: What did Rohit do with Ganga's tiffin?
qa.a: He threw it on the floor.

qa.q: What was Ganga worried about when she asked, "Will he be angry?"
qa.a: She was afraid that telling would make Rohit angrier and the bullying worse.

qa.q: Which part of Bhavna Ma'am's reply mattered most?
qa.a: Saying "I believe you" and then acting that day, by talking to Rohit and his parents and sitting near Ganga at lunch.

qa.q: How does Bhavna Ma'am see Ganga's courage in telling?
qa.a: She sees it as brave and important, and thanks her so Ganga knows speaking up works.

grounding: A young girl tells her teacher about daily bullying, is believed, and feels safe when the teacher acts that same day.

passage: At the village school, Irfan pushed the smaller boys off the tyre swing, one after another. He stood tall on it and laughed. When Bhavna Ma'am came, he was pushing little Chotu. "Irfan, stop. Pushing is not allowed." He sat out for ten minutes. Then she sat beside him on the bench. "You seem sad lately." Irfan kicked the dust. "Abba went to the city for work." "You miss him." Irfan nodded, his eyes wet. "Tomorrow, will you help me hold the swing for the little ones? Strong hands can help, too."

qa.q: What did Irfan push the smaller boys off?
qa.a: He pushed them off the tyre swing.

qa.q: What might Irfan be feeling underneath his pushing?
qa.a: He felt sad and was missing his Abba, who went to the city for work; pushing made him feel powerful for a moment.

qa.q: How did Bhavna Ma'am combine a limit with warmth?
qa.a: She stopped the pushing and gave him time out, then sat with him, noticed his sadness and offered him a way to be strong by helping.

qa.q: How might Chotu see Irfan holding the swing tomorrow?
qa.a: He may feel wary at first, then relieved to find Irfan helping instead of pushing.

grounding: A young boy who pushes smaller children is given a firm limit and a warm adult who notices his sadness and shows him another way to feel strong.

passage: In a kindergarten in Oslo, Ingrid kept pushing the smaller children out of the playhouse. "My house! Get out!" She looked strong and pleased. Clara, the teacher, stopped her. "Ingrid, no pushing. The playhouse is for everyone." Ingrid pushed again. Clara moved her gently to a bench. Then she sat beside her. "Where did you learn 'Get out'?" Ingrid shrugged. "My big brother says it. He pushes me off the sofa." Clara nodded. "Being strong can mean being the house captain who lets people in." At pick-up, Clara told Ingrid's father what she had said.

qa.q: What did Ingrid shout at the smaller children?
qa.a: She shouted, "My house! Get out!"

qa.q: What might Ingrid feel underneath looking strong and pleased?
qa.a: She may feel small and pushed around herself, copying her big brother so she can feel powerful for once.

qa.q: Why did Clara do more than just punish Ingrid?
qa.a: Only punishing would not show her another way; Clara held the limit, asked where the words came from and offered a kinder way to feel strong.

qa.q: How might Ingrid's father feel after Clara talks to him at pick-up?
qa.a: He may be surprised and concerned, and want to help both his children play more gently at home.

grounding: A young girl pushes smaller children to feel powerful, copying her brother, and a teacher sets firm limits and teaches another way to feel strong.
